record.title: Independent Gaussian rounding preserves the conditional mean

aligned_passages.text:
The full-support manuscript proves that an admissible integrable minimizer
of the zero-temperature Parisi functional for the pure zero-field
Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model has Stieltjes support equal to every overlap
scale in [0,1). The proof turns a hypothetical support gap into a constant
interval for the order parameter. Variational contact at the ends of that
interval conflicts with a strict curvature inequality inside it. Along the
auxiliary diffusion, the spatial gradient of the value function is a bounded
martingale. Full support makes this martingale's second moment equal to time;
its terminal correlation with Brownian motion gives the ground-state value.
The manuscript's further argument gives a smooth Stieltjes density, strictly
positive on $(0,1)$, and no atom at zero. Sections 9.1–9.2 derive this stronger
ordinary conclusion separately from the selected formal support statement.

This record reconstructs those arguments and follows the finite Gaussian
approximation into the separate QAOA manuscript. The latter claims that
finite deterministic circuits approach the SK optimum when system size tends
to infinity before circuit depth increases. Its circuit construction needs
additional approximation, synthesis, seed-removal and transfer arguments.
The two formal statements concern full support and scalar value
consequences; neither states QAOA circuit convergence. Their verification
scope is described at the end. See [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main] and
[OpenAI (2026b), Theorem 1.1][q-intro].

### 2.5 Order of approximation

The same symbol for a small error must not conceal changing background
objects. The following account fixes those objects before the indicated
limit. A single admissible minimiser and its associated diffusion are
retained throughout the scalar construction.

**Compact-strip regularity.** Fix a derivative order $k\ge1$, a cutoff
$T<1$ and a common coefficient $L^1$ bound. Coefficients converge in $L^1$
within that bound; spatial derivatives converge uniformly on the strip.

**Shape inequalities on a plateau.** Fix the height $c>0$ and a closed
interior neighbourhood. Choose step coefficients equal to $c$ there and
smooth terminal values with $M_m\ge\|\gamma_m\|_\infty$ and
$M_m\to\infty$. The coefficient and terminal approximations may be
chosen as one compatible sequence.

**First variation.** Fix $\gamma$, a feasible $\eta\in L^1$ and initially
$\epsilon>0$. Remove the terminal cutoff before letting
$\epsilon\downarrow0$. The terminal remainder divided by $\epsilon$ is
bounded by an $L^1$ tail of $\eta$.

**Terminal value.** Keep the chosen minimiser and diffusion fixed. Bounded
martingale convergence and integrability of $\gamma$ justify
$t\uparrow1$; no terminal derivative bound is needed.

**Finite Gaussian coefficients.** Fix $\gamma,X$ and $T<1$. Refine $N$
using the fixed-strip bounds, then control the remaining value tail by $1-T$.

For the plateau transfer, tail estimates for a fixed approximant may depend
on that approximant. The passage to the limit uses the integrated
polynomial in the scaled second, third and fourth spatial derivatives of
the value function and the common strip bounds; it does not require
uniform bounds on the auxiliary density scores. Sections 3 and 4 explain
the variation and plateau-transfer arguments, and §7 gives a complete scalar error
budget. The further choices used to produce a circuit appear in §8.6.
[OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.1, Lemma 6.1, Proposition 5.1 and
Proposition 7.2][fs-main].

**Proposition 7.1 (finite Gaussian approximation).** For a fixed minimizer and its diffusion, the construction below has positive active normalizers for all sufficiently fine meshes at every fixed $0i$ vanishes on conditioning on the first $j-1$ coordinates; and the $j=i$ term is $\sqrt\Delta\,\mathbb E a(t_{i-1},Y_{i-1})$. Also $\mathbb E[M_Ng_j]=\sqrt\Delta/c_j$ by orthonormality. Bessel's inequality applied separately to the orthonormal family $(g_j)$ and to the family $(Z_i)$ gives the vector estimates. Their union need not be orthogonal: $$ (A_j)_{j=1}^N=(\sqrt\Delta/c_j)_{j=1}^N+o_{\ell^2}(1), $$ $$ (B_i)_{i=1}^N= (\sqrt\Delta\,\mathbb E a(t_{i-1},Y_{i-1}))_{i=1}^N+o_{\ell^2}(1). $$ Coordinatewise errors would not control a sum of growing length. Put $$ e_N=\|u(T,Y_N)-M_N\|_2,\quad \alpha_j=\sqrt\Delta/c_j,\quad \beta_j=\sqrt\Delta\,\mathbb E a(t_{j-1},Y_{j-1}) \quad(1\le j\le N). $$ The fixed-$T$ Euler argument gives $e_N\to0$. Bessel's inequality gives $\|A_{1:N}-\alpha\|_2,\|B_{1:N}-\beta\|_2\le e_N$. Also $\|B_{1:N}\|_2\le1$ and $\|\alpha\|_2\le C_T$ for sufficiently large $N$, with $C_T$ independent of the mesh. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $$ \begin{aligned} \left|\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}(A_jB_{j+1}-\alpha_j\beta_{j+1})\right| &\le\|A-\alpha\|_2\|B_{2:N}\|_2 +\|\alpha_{1:N-1}\|_2\|B-\beta\|_2\\ &\le(1+C_T)e_N. \end{aligned} $$ The unindexed differences in this inequality use coordinates $1,\ldots,N$; restricting to the indicated subvector only decreases their norms. The rounding coordinate contributes at most $|A_NB_{N+1}|\le e_N+\sqrt\Delta/c_N$. Thus the dimension-free estimate is $$ \left|\sum_{j=0}^NA_jB_{j+1} -\Delta\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\frac{\mathbb E a(t_j,Y_j)}{c_j}\right| \le(2+C_T)e_N+\frac{\sqrt\Delta}{c_N}\longrightarrow0. $$ The index shift selects the Hessian at $t_j$; $Z_{N+1}$ serves rounding rather than another Euler increment. This estimate is a fixed-strip scalar correspondence, not a circuit energy identity. Hence $$ \sum_{j=0}^NA_jB_{j+1} =\Delta\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\frac{\mathbb E a(t_j,Y_j)}{c_j}+o(1) \longrightarrow\int_0^T\mathbb E a(t,X_t)\,dt. $$ The same vector estimates also give an unshifted sum with this limit: $$ \left|\sum_{j=1}^N A_jB_j-\sum_{j=1}^N\alpha_j\beta_j\right| \le(1+C_T)e_N\longrightarrow0, $$ $$ \sum_{j=1}^N A_jB_j =\Delta\sum_{j=1}^N \frac{\mathbb E a(t_{j-1},Y_{j-1})}{c_j}+o(1) \longrightarrow\int_0^T\mathbb E a(t,X_t)\,dt. $$ The latter is a left Riemann sum: $c_j\to1$ uniformly and the Euler coupling replaces $Y_{j-1}$ by $X_{t_{j-1}}$. Equal continuum limits therefore do not identify the finite expression needed by the circuit. The rooted energy calculation in §8.1 selects the adjacent pairing; the two finite pairings can differ, as [§10.4](#one-step-example) shows. Only afterward let $T\uparrow1$, obtaining $P_*$. The mesh count $N$ is unrelated to the spin-system size $n$. As in [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 7.2][fs-cons], these coefficients describe a finite Gaussian function, not yet a circuit on finite SK disorder. The QAOA scalar input also uses the tail estimate $0\le P_*-\int_0^T\mathbb E a(t,X_t)\,dt\le1-T$, from nonnegative curvature and $\mathbb E a^2=1$. This estimate and the fixed-strip regularity facts must be retained beside the coefficient limit; they are not all clauses of the selected finite-Gaussian statement. They enter the construction in [OpenAI (2026b), §3][q-classical]. Thus, for every accuracy, the same chosen minimizer supplies a cutoff $T$ and then one finite function $F_N$ with $|S_{T,N}-P_*|$ below that accuracy. This is the finite scalar input. Turning it into spins for a finite SK matrix uses the separate AMP theorem in §9.4; turning it into a common QAOA word uses §§8.1–8.6. Neither operation is part of the Gaussian limit.

### 7.1 Error estimates at a fixed cutoff Fix the minimizer first and then $T<1$. The bounds below have constants depending on that minimizer and strip; they give an $N^{-1/2}$ rate there, not a rate uniform as $T\uparrow1$. Those derivative bounds are finite but have not been supplied as numerical inputs to an algorithm for choosing a mesh. The calculation is an ordinary deduction from the source's strip estimates, beyond the qualitative selected formal statement. Write $S_{T,N}=\sum_{j=0}^N A_jB_{j+1}$ and $f(t)=\mathbb E a(t,X_t)$, so $0\le f(t)\le1$. On the fixed strip let $K_T=\sup_{t\le T,x}|a(t,x)|$ and choose a spatial Lipschitz constant $L_T$ for $a$. Define $$ \delta_N=\max_{0\le j\le N}\|Y_j-X_{t_j}\|_2,\qquad d_N=\max_{1\le j\le N} \left|\mathbb E a(t_{j-1},Y_{j-1})^2-1\right|. $$ These errors have a rate at each fixed strip, even if $\gamma$ has jumps. Put $\Gamma=\gamma(T)$ and $V=\gamma(T)-\gamma(0)$. Bounded spatial derivatives and the PDE give temporal Lipschitz constants $$ J=\tfrac12\|u_{xx}\|_\infty+\Gamma K_T,\qquad H=\tfrac12\|a_{xx}\|_\infty+\Gamma(K_T^2+L_T) $$ for $u$ and $a$, respectively, on this strip. No derivative of $\gamma$ is used. Brownian coupling gives $\|X_s-X_{\pi_N(s)}\|_2\le\sqrt\Delta+\Gamma\Delta$. Subtract the Euler and diffusion equations and split the drift difference on $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$ as $$ \gamma(s)\bigl(u(s,X_s)-u(t_j,Y_j)\bigr) +\bigl(\gamma(s)-\gamma(t_j)\bigr)u(t_j,Y_j). $$ Put $A_T=\int_0^T\gamma(s)\,ds\le1$ and $w_j=\int_{t_j}^{t_{j+1}}\gamma(s)\,ds$. Taking a pathwise maximum over grid times, Minkowski and discrete Gronwall give, with $$ R_N=A_TK_T\sqrt\Delta+ [A_T(J+\Gamma K_T)+V]\Delta, $$ the bound $$ \delta_N\le\left\|\max_{j\le N}|Y_j-X_{t_j}|\right\|_2 \le e^{K_TA_T}R_N\le e^{K_T}R_N. $$ The recurrence weights the preceding maximal norm on interval $j$ by $K_Tw_j$; their sum is $K_TA_T$. The term $V\Delta$ is the monotone quadrature bound for the coefficient. For the martingale residual, Itô isometry and the same increment estimate give $$ e_N\le K_T\delta_N+ \sqrt T\{L_T\delta_N+L_T\sqrt\Delta+(H+\Gamma L_T)\Delta\}. $$ Thus $\delta_N,e_N=O_{\gamma,T}(\sqrt\Delta)$. These are deductions from the compact-strip bounds and stochastic identities, not quantitative clauses of the selected Lean statement. Since $a$ is bounded and Lipschitz, $d_N\le2K_TL_T\delta_N\to0$. Whenever $d_N\le1/2$, $$ \sqrt{2/3}\le c_j\le\sqrt2,\qquad |1/c_j-1|\le d_N,\qquad \|\alpha\|_2\le\sqrt{T(1+d_N)}. $$ These estimates give an explicit sufficient condition for all the required normalisers to be positive. They do not assume positivity for every coarse mesh. The first-moment identity in §6 makes $f=m$ nonincreasing, with $f(0)=1$. Its right Riemann sum therefore satisfies $$ 0\le I(T)-\Delta\sum_{j=1}^N f(t_j) \le\Delta\bigl(f(0)-f(T)\bigr). $$ Removing the last term adds $\Delta f(T)$, so $0\le I(T)-\Delta\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}f(t_j)\le\Delta$. The difference between the shifted interior sum and the integral is bounded by $$ \left|\Delta\sum_{j=1}^{N-1} \frac{\mathbb E a(t_j,Y_j)}{c_j}-\int_0^T f(t)\,dt\right| \le TK_Td_N+TL_T\delta_N+\Delta. $$ The first two terms replace the normalisers and Euler positions; the last is the preceding monotone quadrature estimate. Combining this with the vector and rounding-endpoint estimate gives $$ \begin{aligned} |S_{T,N}-P_*| \le{}&(1-T)m(T) +\bigl(2+\sqrt{T(1+d_N)}\bigr)e_N +\sqrt{\Delta(1+d_N)}\\ &+TK_Td_N+TL_T\delta_N+\Delta . \end{aligned} $$ In particular, for each fixed minimizer and $T<1$ there are finite $C_{\gamma,T}$ and $N_0(\gamma,T)$ such that $$ |S_{T,N}-P_*|\le(1-T)m(T)+C_{\gamma,T}\sqrt{T/N} \qquad(N\ge N_0(\gamma,T)). $$ The constants are not uniform as $T\uparrow1$. The [coefficient budget](#coefficient-budget) bounds $\int\gamma$ and $\gamma$ on each fixed strip, but numerical bounds for all strip derivative constants and an effective mesh threshold are not supplied. The scalar tail bound $(1-T)m(T)\le1-T$ uses only monotonicity of the first moment; Proposition 6.2 further makes it $o(1-T)$. All terms after this scalar tail tend to zero at each fixed $T<1$. Given a scalar tolerance $\zeta>0$, first choose $T$ with $1-T<\zeta/2$, then choose $N_0(\gamma,T,\zeta)$ so that their sum is below $\zeta/2$ for every $N\ge N_0$. This is the required finite choice of a Gaussian spin. The formula exposes the errors; it does not supply numerical values of $K_T,L_T,\delta_N,e_N$ or an effective mesh threshold. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.1][fs-reg]; [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 7.2][fs-cons]. A diagonal can be chosen using these thresholds. For prescribed $T_m\uparrow1$, choose increasing $N_m$ large enough to make the mesh-dependent part of the fixed-$T_m$ bound less than $1/m$. An arbitrary increasing mesh schedule does not follow from the iterated limit alone. For example, the scalar array $$ h(T,N)=\min\{1,[N(1-T)]^{-1}\} $$ tends to zero in $N$ at every fixed $T<1$, but $h(1-1/N,N)=1$ for every $N\ge2$. This is an illustration of the quantifier issue, not an asserted error law for the SK construction.

On a single spin, let $Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ and
$X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$; $Z_i$ and $X_i$ act on spin $i$
and as the identity on the other spins. Also set
$Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$ and
$|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$.
Then $X|\pm\rangle=\pm|\pm\rangle$ and $Z|+\rangle=|-\rangle$. The cost and mixer are
$$
C_{n,J}=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}Z_iZ_j,\qquad B_n=\sum_iX_i.
$$
The two evolutions act differently:
$$
e^{-i\theta C_{n,J}}|\sigma\rangle
 =e^{-i\theta H_n(\sigma)}|\sigma\rangle,
\qquad
e^{-i\beta B_n}=\prod_{i=1}^n(\cos\beta\,I-i\sin\beta\,X_i).
$$
The cost evolution changes phases while preserving spin-basis probabilities;
the mixer combines amplitudes of different spin configurations. Cost evolution
alone leaves the initial uniform probabilities unchanged, and a mixer applied
first only multiplies $|+\rangle^{\otimes n}$ by $e^{-in\beta}$.
Alternating them lets the cost-dependent phases change subsequent measurement
probabilities. [Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou (2022), §2,
equations (1)–(6)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.08187v4).

A depth-$p$ state, with $p$ counting cost–mixer pairs, is
$$
|\psi_{n,p,J}(\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta)\rangle
=e^{-i\beta_pB_n}e^{-i\gamma_pC_{n,J}}\cdots
 e^{-i\beta_1B_n}e^{-i\gamma_1C_{n,J}}|+\rangle^{\otimes n}.
$$
Here the real angle vectors $\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta$ are
deterministic; $\boldsymbol\gamma$ is separate from the Parisi coefficient
$\gamma(t)$. A *word* means a finite ordered product of cost and mixer
exponentials. Its pattern and angles are fixed independently of $n,J$;
its cost operator depends on $n,J$. Define
$$
v_p(\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta)
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E_J
 \langle\psi_{n,p,J}|C_{n,J}|\psi_{n,p,J}\rangle,
\qquad Q_p=\sup_{\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^p}v_p.
$$
The fixed-depth, fixed-angle infinite-size limit is the input from
Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou; it does not contain the later depth
conclusion; see [Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.08187v4).
The source target is $\lim_{p\to\infty}Q_p=P_*$. Its needed lower
bound has the literal quantifiers
$$
\forall\varepsilon>0\quad\exists p\in\mathbb N,
\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^p:
\quad\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E_J
\langle\psi_{n,p,J}|C_{n,J}|\psi_{n,p,J}\rangle
\ge P_*-\varepsilon.
$$
The same finite list of gates and angles is used for every $n,J$; this is
a limiting expected-energy conclusion. A cost expectation is bounded above by its
maximum eigenvalue, and zero-angle padding makes $Q_p$ nondecreasing.
It therefore suffices to construct one finite word for every accuracy.
Fixed-instance convergence at increasing depth is a different quantifier
order. Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann's original QAOA argument obtains that
convergence by adiabatic evolution and its Trotter approximation, with depth
allowed to depend on the instance; it does not supply the size-independent
word required here. [Farhi–Goldstone–Gutmann (2014), equation (10) and
§VI, pp. 10–11](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.4028v1);
[OpenAI (2026b), Theorem 1.1][q-intro].

The construction first describes local operations on a large tree, where
neighbouring subtrees supply Gaussian inputs. Temporary random labels let
those operations implement the finite classical function of §7. The hard
steps are to implement its aggregations using cost and mixer gates, and
then to replace every use of the labels by ordinary gates while preserving
the energy. Only the resulting ordinary word is transferred to SK.

The choices are nested: fix $\varepsilon$, choose $T<1$, choose a finite
mesh, fix the bounded classical formula and helper probabilities, then
choose the finite gate approximations and remove the seeds. The constants
in a replacement may depend on the surrounding word and on those positive
helper probabilities. [§8.6](#qaoa-assembly-detail) collects the error
allocation before the final $n\to\infty$ limit.
The principal circuit inputs can be read as four local lemmas. Their
proofs remain in the cited manuscript; §§8.2–8.5 reconstruct the
mechanisms and show where each hypothesis enters.

**Smooth replacement.** Fix the height, a finite expression and channel
list, and the required derivatives. Uniform recursive weighted bounds,
convergence of operators and adjoints, and strongly commuting signals with
the stated joint exponential bounds permit substitution inside a fixed
surrounding sequence in the exclusion-gate class defined in §8.2. Constants depend on that fixed family. This is the input
used in §8.3 to replace classical aggregates by finite gates; see
[the foundations, smooth topology and gate calculus][q-gate-calculus].

**Helper contraction and synthesis.** Fix a bounded, finite, type-excluded
odd formula, zero on helpers, and positive helper masses. The contraction
converges smoothly at every cut and for the specified responses. For each
$\eta>0$, finite seeded synthesis gives
$$
\mathcal E(v)\ge\mathcal E(m)-2\eta-2\sqrt{p_H}.
$$
Section 8.4 receives this one fixed seeded word. The source inputs are the
[synthesis statements][q-synthesis-statement] and
[helper theorem][q-helper-statement].

**Seed removal.** Fix that finite seeded word and an energy tolerance.
Reuse the same Gaussian at every occurrence on a vertex. Packet control and
the one-particle comparison then produce one finite ordinary word with the
required energy error. The [seed-removal theorem][q-seed-statement] supplies
an energy conclusion, not merely convergence of seed marginals. It makes the
ordinary-word transfer in §8.5 applicable.

**Fixed-word transfer.** Fix one ordinary word and all its angles before
either size or degree varies. Its positive tree scaled-edge limit equals
its SK expected-energy limit, with the convention conversion in §8.5.
This [fixed-word transfer][q-transfer] closes the thermodynamic-first
theorem in §8.6.

### 8.1 Rooted realisation and the observable it preserves The fixed-depth spin–boson representation has an antecedent in [Boulebnane et al., Theorem 2 (informal), equations (10)–(11), p. 3][spin-boson]: as the degree grows with depth fixed, the symmetric tree state converges to a spin coupled to finitely many bosonic modes. The manuscript credits that representation, then proves the occupation, insertion and surrounding-circuit estimates needed below. Its additional task is to control the energy observable and substitutions inside a circuit, beyond identifying a limiting state. [OpenAI (2026b), §2][q-fock]. The immediate task is to realise the finite Gaussian spin from §7 in a space where its shifted correlation sum becomes an energy observable. We will identify that sum with a rooted quadratic form, then relate the same form to the scaled edge energy of a fixed circuit; §8.5 supplies the final transfer to SK. For an ordinary depth-$p$ word, this tree calculation uses only finitely many spins. Conjugate $Z_iZ_j$ backwards through the circuit. A mixer rotates the spins already in its support without enlarging that support. In a cost layer all edge factors commute, so factors disjoint from the current support commute past the other factors and cancel. The remaining factors enlarge support by at most one graph step. After $p$ pairs, the edge expectation therefore depends only on its radius-$p$ backward light cone. On the $(D+1)$-regular tree this contains at most $2\sum_{r=0}^pD^r$ vertices; the spins outside factor out of the product-state expectation. Thus fixed depth gives fixed tree height, although the number of children grows with $D$. This locality explains the finite tree calculation; the equality with dense SK is the separate transfer theorem in §8.5. [Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann (2014), §II, equations (14)–(26)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.4028v1). On a rooted tree, factor a circuit as $U=(\bigotimes_jU_j)u$, where each $U_j$ contains operations wholly in child subtree $j$. Conjugating a root observable $P$ reduces to $u^*Pu$; its insertion vector is $u^*Pu\,\mathrm{vac}$, centered when its vacuum mean is zero. This factorization is why child operations enter the recursion below. The first change of setting preserves a specified quadratic form. At height zero the pointed space is $\mathsf k=\mathbb C^2\otimes L^2(\text{seed})$, with distinguished vector $\omega=|+\rangle\otimes1$. Recursively, $$ \mathcal H_0=\mathsf k,\qquad \mathcal H_{h+1}=\mathsf k\otimes\Gamma_s(\mathcal H_h^\circ), $$ where $\mathcal H_h^\circ$ is the orthogonal complement of the vacuum and $\Gamma_s$ is symmetric Fock space. A particle here is one child subtree whose state differs from its vacuum. It is not one physical spin. The occupation embedding identifies a symmetric state with $m$ nonvacuum children among $D$ available children with its $m$-particle vector, using the factor $\binom Dm^{-1/2}$. Adding empty descendants gives compatible embeddings between heights. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, pointed spaces and occupation embeddings][q-fock]. For a child direction $f$, write $q(f)=a^*(f)+a(f)$ and $W(f)=e^{iq(f)}$. Explicitly, $\Gamma_s(H)=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}H^{\otimes_s m}$, with vacuum $\Omega$ in sector zero. On sector $m$, $a^*(f)\psi=\sqrt{m+1}\operatorname{Sym}(f\otimes\psi)$, and $a(f)$ is its adjoint. The number operator is multiplication by $m$; more generally $d\Gamma(A)$ sums $A$ over those $m$ child factors. The vacuum characteristic function $\langle\Omega,e^{itq(f)}\Omega\rangle=e^{-t^2\|f\|^2/2}$ fixes the Gaussian normalization. For any finite list of fixed centred real child vectors, their parent positions $\mathsf G(f)=q(f)$ are jointly centred Gaussian; for $f,g$, $$ \mathbb E[\mathsf G(f)\mathsf G(g)]=\langle f,g\rangle, \qquad \|[\mathsf G(f)-\mathsf G(g)]\mathrm{vac}\|=\|f-g\|. $$ The directions are fixed elements of the child space, even when their values depend on the child's Gaussian coordinates. The receiving root's own seed is a separate, independent tensor factor. The root shift $$ \mathsf Lf=\omega\otimes a^*(f)\Omega $$ is an isometry on centred vectors, and is extended by zero on the vacuum. Its adjoint extracts the root-vacuum, one-child component, including a constant receiving-root seed. For a classical function of orthonormal Gaussian positions, this is its first Gaussian chaos. These covariance, independence and projection properties have distinct roles in the next calculation. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, root shift and classical first chaos][q-root-energy] [OpenAI (2026b), §2, classical Gaussian positions][q-gaussian]. Start with the standard root seed $g_0=S$ and recursively set $Z_{j+1}=\mathsf G(g_j)$. Suppose $g_0,\ldots,g_{j-1}$ are centred orthonormal vectors. The joint Gaussian law of their lifts and the covariance identity give independent standard normals $Z_1,\ldots,Z_j$. In the scalar construction of §7, the multiplier of $Z_j$ in $g_j$ depends only on its predecessors. Conditional centring therefore makes $g_j$ orthogonal to $g_1,\ldots,g_{j-1}$, and the chosen normaliser $c_j$ gives unit norm. Independence of the receiving-root seed gives orthogonality to $g_0$. This closes the induction. Compatible height embeddings ensure that the earlier variables are the same variables when the formula is embedded at greater height. Oddness of $u$ and evenness of $a$ make $Y_j$ and $g_j$ odd under simultaneous seed reversal. The extra centred rounding variable $2F_{\rm G}(Z_{N+1})-1$ is odd as well, so $F_N$ is centred. It is independent of the receiving-root seed, hence $\langle F_N,g_0\rangle=0=A_0$. With $A_j,B_{j+1}$ as in §7, first-chaos projection gives $$ \mathsf L^*F_N=\sum_{j=0}^NB_{j+1}g_j,\qquad \mathcal E(F_N):=\operatorname{Re}\langle F_N,\mathsf LF_N\rangle =\sum_{j=0}^NA_jB_{j+1}. $$ Thus the construction identifies both the scalar law and the required rooted energy. The Gaussian covariance rule does not declare distinct calculations on shared descendant subtrees independent. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, “A finite Gaussian formula and its rooted energy”][q-rooted-classical]. The connection to an edge observable is another statement. Let $f_D$ be centred, invariant under rooted permutations of complete child subtrees, and supported at a fixed finite radius. Suppose its occupation embedding converges strongly to $v$, with a uniformly bounded expected top-generation occupation $\langle f_D,\mathsf Nf_D\rangle$. Put $M=D+1$ and $R_M=\sqrt{1-\mathsf N/M}$. To see the decomposition, delete the distinguished edge and project onto the vacuum on either resulting half-tree. There are four pairings. The vacuum–vacuum pairing is zero by centring. If only one side is excited, the other side forces the root and all remaining branches into their vacuum; root symmetry gives the term $M^{-1/2}\langle\mathsf L^*f_D,R_Mf_D\rangle$ or its conjugate. In the pairing where both sides are excited, each projected vector has squared norm $M^{-1}\langle f_D,\mathsf Nf_D\rangle$ by symmetry among the $M$ branches. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds their pairing by that same quantity. Finally, deleting one vacuum child multiplies the $m$-particle sector by $\sqrt{\binom{M-1}{m}/\binom{M}{m}}=\sqrt{1-m/M}$, which identifies $R_M$. Thus the exact edge decomposition is $$ \langle f_{D,i},f_{D,j}\rangle =\frac2{\sqrt M}\operatorname{Re}\langle\mathsf L^*f_D,R_Mf_D\rangle +\varepsilon_D, \qquad |\varepsilon_D|\le\frac{\langle f_D,\mathsf Nf_D\rangle}{M}. $$ Vacuum deletion also gives $\|R_Mf_D-f_D\|^2\le M^{-1}\langle f_D,\mathsf Nf_D\rangle$. Consequently, $$ \lim_{D\to\infty}\frac{\sqrt D}{2} \langle f_{D,i},f_{D,j}\rangle=\mathcal E(v). $$ Strong convergence alone does not control the scaled remainder. The occupation estimate is supplied later for the relevant finite circuits. The occupation assumption cannot be dropped merely because vectors converge in norm. For orthogonal unit vectors $e_m$ in sector $m$, $\psi_k=\sqrt{1-1/k}\,\Omega+k^{-1/2}e_{k^2}$ tends to $\Omega$ in norm, whereas $\langle\psi_k,\mathsf N\psi_k\rangle=k$. The elementary continuity bound $$ |\mathcal E(v)-\mathcal E(w)| \le(\|v\|+\|w\|)\|v-w\| $$ will control every subsequent approximation after the observable has been identified. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Energy as a root shift,” including its exact finite-degree decomposition][q-root-energy]. The three identifications use different information: First, passing from the finite Gaussian formula to the rooted classical sector preserves the joint Gaussian law and the same $F_N$. This uses covariance, conditional centring and independence of the receiving-root seed. Second, the root-vacuum and first-chaos projection identify the energy itself: $\mathcal E(F_N)=S_{T,N}$. ### 5.1 A martingale formula for the ground-state value The support identities give a scalar representation of $P_*$. Set $M_t=u(t,X_t)$, the bounded gradient martingale satisfying $dM_t=a(t,X_t)\,dB_t$. The quadratic variations distinguish the two Hessian moments: $$ d\langle M\rangle_t=a(t,X_t)^2\,dt, \qquad d\langle M,B\rangle_t=a(t,X_t)\,dt. $$ Full support gives $\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$, hence each increment $M_t-M_s$ has unconditional variance $t-s$. This normalises the discrete increments below. The first moment of $a$ instead gives covariance with the driving noise. Let $U$ be the almost-sure and $L^2$ limit of $M_t$. The value identity is $$ P_*=\mathbb E[UB_1] =\int_0^1\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)]\,dt. \tag{10} $$ Boundedness gives $|U|\leq1$, while $\mathbb E M_t^2\to1$ gives $\mathbb E U^2=1$; therefore $U^2=1$ almost surely. To see the cancellation behind (10), the terminal convergence of the convex value functions gives $UX_1=|X_1|$ (the equality is automatic on $X_1=0$), while Itô's formula gives $\mathcal P(\gamma)=\mathbb E|X_1|-\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt$. Multiplying $X_1=B_1+\int_0^1\gamma(t)M_t\,dt$ by $U$ cancels that integral because $\mathbb E[UM_t]=t$. The Parisi formula then gives (10). The endpoint limits and stochastic-integral covariance are proved in [OpenAI (2026a), Corollary 7.1][FS] and the long record, [§6, “Recovering the value from a martingale”](../long/reasoning-record.md#scalar-value-identities). This argument uses full support, not the density corollary. In particular, convexity and Cauchy–Schwarz give $0\leq\mathbb E a\leq1$, so $$ 0\leq P_*-\int_0^T\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)]\,dt\leq1-T. $$ One can therefore fix the terminal cutoff before discretising the diffusion. The gradient-martingale and value methods have antecedents in [Montanari, preprint v2, Lemmas 3.2–3.4][Montanari], under its positive-temperature support assumption, and in the zero-temperature calculations of [El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke, preprint v1, Lemmas 6.5 and 6.13][EAMS]. [Sellke, preprint v4, Proposition 3.10 and Lemma 3.11, p. 17][Sellke] gives the closely related finite-cutoff cancellation by applying Itô's formula to $\Phi$ and $x\Phi_x$. ### 5.2 The classical algorithm Full support and existence give an attained, strictly increasing minimiser in the monotone zero-temperature class. This is Assumption 2 of [El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke, preprint v1][EAMS]. Their Corollary 2.2 then gives, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, a randomised algorithm returning a configuration within $\varepsilon n$ of the finite SK maximum with probability tending to one over couplings and algorithmic randomness. Its cost is $C(\varepsilon)n^2$ real-arithmetic operations with the prescribed scalar functions and normalisers available; this includes no separate numerical-preprocessing or finite-precision bound. [OpenAI (2026a), Corollary 7.3][FS] and [long §9.4](../long/reasoning-record.md#classical-algorithm-consequence) check the Gaussian convention and operation count. Chen already records the classical consequence in [§1, p. 4][Chen]. Their incremental approximate message-passing iterates use the coupling matrix. Their scalar description uses the martingale multiplier and state drift $$ u_{\rm EAMS}(t,x)=a(t,x),\qquad v_{\rm EAMS}(t,x)=\gamma(t)u(t,x). $$ Thus their noise multiplier is the Hessian, whereas our $u$ is the gradient. The bounded martingale $M_t$ and $\mathbb E a^2=1$ give the required variance normalisation. With the fixed-strip regularity and discretisation estimates, [their Theorem 2][EAMS] achieves energy arbitrarily close to the truncated first-moment integral in (10). Strict positivity of the density is unnecessary.
